overview: This record follows Serbia after international recognition of its independence in 1878, through its kingdom and the First World War. Banks, water systems, museums and universities developed alongside parliamentary conflict and devastating war. It ends around the transition into a larger South Slav state, not the end of Serbian communities.

periods.title: Independent principality
periods.summary: Recognition preceded the proclamation of the kingdom in 1882.

periods.title: Kingdom and institutional change
periods.summary: Banking and parliamentary institutions developed before the disruption of the First World War.

periods.title: A larger South Slav state
periods.summary: The 1918 unification changed the state framework and its money.

items.text: Before Belgrade’s water-supply system opened in 1892, Knez Mihailova Street depended on courtyard wells and the Delijska Fountain. Fetching water was part of household work. The new system changed a practical daily task, not merely the city’s appearance.

Electric street lighting arrived in Belgrade in 1891, with an early lantern at the corner of Kralja Petra and Knez Mihailova. Lighting a street extended useful public space after dark, although one lamp does not prove every household had electricity.

After recognition of independence, Serbia minted gold twenty-dinar coins in 1879. In 1884 its new national bank issued hundred-dinar notes payable in gold. Paper money depended on confidence in an institution as well as the paper’s printed design.

The bank began operations in July 1884, following legislation passed the previous year. It supplied credit and handled currency issuance. Establishing an institution required rules and staff, not simply printing an impressive-looking note.

Привилегована Народна банка Краљевине Србије means “Privileged National Bank of the Kingdom of Serbia.” This Serbian Cyrillic title is attested in the bank’s catalogue of a book published in Belgrade in 1909, covering its first twenty-five years.

Milutin Milanković joined the University of Belgrade in 1909 and shared an office with Mihailo Petrović. One taught applied mathematics and the other theoretical mathematics. A scientific community grew through colleagues teaching and exchanging ideas.

In 1912 Mladen Berić defended the university’s first doctoral dissertation in mathematical sciences before a commission including Petrović and Milanković. Advanced education required teachers able to train a new generation, not just individuals making discoveries alone.

Petrović constructed a hydro-integrator in 1900, a calculating instrument using water, and received a bronze medal at the Paris exhibition. Mathematical work could take the form of a physical device as well as equations on a blackboard.

The National Museum had been founded in 1844 to collect and preserve antiquities, before this map interval. Its continued work made objects available for study. A museum collection is assembled through choices, rather than being a complete sample of everyone’s past.

sections.title: Political participation and care during war

items.text: The constitutions of 1888 and 1903 shaped parliamentary life and the role of parties. The Assembly’s history records changes in the balance between monarchs, governments and representatives. Rules about participation had consequences for how power could be challenged.

Assembly meetings took place in several buildings and cities, including a school in Niš. During wartime, public institutions had to adapt their location and routines. Parliamentary history therefore includes ordinary rooms temporarily used for extraordinary decisions.

Nurse Ljubica Luković cared for wounded people from Serbian and opposing armies. A Red Cross notice records that she worked at Valjevo during the 1915 typhus epidemic and died after becoming infected. Her story shows the human labour behind wartime healthcare.

ending.text: Serbia entered the new South Slav kingdom in 1918. Its independent kingdom was incorporated into a larger state, while communities and institutions continued in a changed framework. The atlas extends this label to 1920; that endpoint should not turn the 1918 transition into two additional years of unchanged sovereignty.
